Pleasure... well, doc, I'm not really sure how to answer that, to be honest with you. I mean, I don't think I've stopped liking those things, exactly. Like with the community center, I still go down there every other Saturday when I'm off the road. We do the bingo, like I was saying, and sometimes the Sunday pancake breakfasts. But pleasure? Like, a real strong feeling of being happy about it? I don't know. I haven't really noticed feeling much of anything about it either way. It's just something I do. 

And with my wife... she's great. She really is a good woman to put up with my schedule all these years. We'll sit out on the porch when I get back from a long haul down I-95, maybe have a beer or an iced tea, and just watch the cars go by. And I like being with her, I definitely don't want to be anywhere else. But I just don't know if I feel that spark, or that lift, you know? It's not like I'm miserable doing these things with her, I'm not sitting there upset or anything. It's just that everything feels kind of level. Just flat. So, I don't really know if I'm *not* enjoying them, it's just... it's just part of the routine now, I guess. Like checking the tire pressure on the rig before a trip. You just do it because it's what you do, not because you get a big kick out of it. Does that make sense?

Excited... look forward to things. Man, that's a tough one. I mean, I guess I don't really get that feeling of, like, counting down the days on the calendar for something, you know? Like, take vacations, for example. My wife and I, usually once a year, we try to go down to her sister's place in Florida. It's nice down there, near Sarasota. We drive down—I prefer driving, obviously, since I do it for a living, and I don't really like the hassle of the airports with the security lines and the tiny seats where my knees are jammed up against the tray table. Plus, taking the truck means we can pack whatever we want. 

Anyway, when we're getting ready for that trip, she's always buzzing around the house, making packing lists, talking about which restaurants we're going to hit up, buying new sunscreen or whatever. And I'm just... I'm packing the suitcases into the trunk, checking the oil in her sedan, making sure the tire pressure is good for the highway miles. I'm doing the prep, but I don't have that feeling she has. That buzzing feeling. I'm just looking at it like, 'Okay, next week we will be in Florida instead of here.' 

And it's the same with the holidays. Thanksgiving, Christmas. We always have the family over, my side and hers, and it's a full house. I do the turkey—I fry it out in the driveway, been doing it that way for ten years since my brother-in-law got me the fryer setup. I get the oil temperature just right, I make sure the bird is completely thawed so it doesn't explode... I do all the steps. But leading up to it, I'm not sitting there thinking, 'Oh boy, I can't wait for Thanksgiving!' It's just another thing on the schedule. 

I guess I just don't get that spark of anticipation anymore. I don't dread these things, like I said before. I don't sit there wishing I could just cancel the Florida trip or tell everyone to stay home for Christmas. I'll go, I'll do it, I'll fry the turkey, I'll drive the miles to Sarasota. But that feeling of being excited? Like, really looking forward to it? I just don't think I have that gear anymore. It's just... it's just what happens next on the calendar. So, yeah, I guess I don't really feel excited about much of anything.

Ending my life? Lord, no. No, doc. I mean, I get why you have to ask that, I really do. You hear stories, especially in my line of work. Driving long haul, it can get to some guys. You're out there in the cab of the truck, sometimes for days at a time if you're on a bad route, just staring at the asphalt and listening to the hum of those tires, and your mind can go to some pretty dark places if you let it. I knew a guy, a dispatcher out of Omaha about ten years back, who just couldn't take the grind anymore... but that's not me. It's really not. 

Like I've been saying, I'm not sitting around in agony or crying my eyes out or feeling like the world is crashing down on me. It's just that flat feeling. I'm just coasting in neutral. And besides, I could never do something like that to my wife. She's put too much time into me, you know? Thirty years we've been married this coming October, and if I just checked out early, it would leave her with an absolute mess. The mortgage, the truck payments, all those manila folders I was telling you about... she hates doing the paperwork. She'd be completely lost trying to sort out the utility bills and the insurance premiums, and I take my responsibilities seriously. I always have.

How long... well, if I really sit down and trace it back, I guess it's been about three years now. Yeah, three years. It started right around the time my dad passed away. 

That was back in, let's see, it would have been early spring. March. I remember it was March because it was still freezing rain up in the panhandle where I was running a load of lumber, and the roads were just a miserable sheet of ice. I got the call from my sister while I was pulled over at a rest stop. He had been sick for a bit, it was his heart, so it wasn't a total shock, you know? But still, when it actually happens, it changes things. 

I took a couple weeks off work, which I almost never do—I hate leaving my dispatcher hanging—but I had to go help my mom sort out the house and the estate and all that. We had to sell his old Chevy pickup, which honestly broke my heart a little, but she couldn't drive a manual transmission and it was just going to sit there and rust in the driveway. Anyway, we got through the funeral, got the paperwork sorted, and after all the dust settled, I got back in my rig and went back to my routes. 

At first, I figured I was just grieving, you know? Just feeling weighed down because of the funeral and losing the old man. Anyone would feel that way. But then spring turned into summer, and summer into fall, and we had the holidays without him, and that feeling... it just never lifted. It never went away. I kept thinking one morning I'd wake up, brew my coffee, and feel like my old self again—the guy who used to actually whistle while he checked his tire pressure in the morning. But it's been three whole years now of just... coasting. Just that same flat, heavy line every single day since we buried him. So, yeah, I'd say three years is about right.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Sleep? Yeah, sleep's... well, it's not great. I mean, it's not like I'm up all night staring at the ceiling fan going round and round, but it's just not what it used to be. You know, back in the day, my head would hit the pillow and I was out cold until the alarm went off. My wife used to joke that a freight train could drive right through the bedroom and I wouldn't even flinch. But lately... especially on the nights before a run, it's a whole different story.

I'll get into bed, usually around ten, ten-thirty, right after the late local news—I always like to catch the weather report, you know, just to see what kind of mess I might be driving into the next day—and I'll just lie there. I'll be trying to shut my brain off, but instead, I'm just running through the whole route in my head. I'll be thinking about the next day's stops, worrying if the loading dock at the warehouse in Des Moines is going to be backed up again, or if I need to take the bypass around Chicago because of that construction on 94... just all these little details that I shouldn't be sweating at eleven o'clock at night. 

And then, even when I do finally drift off, it's not a deep sleep. It's that light, choppy kind of sleep where you feel like you're half awake the whole time. And then, without fail, I'll wake up around four in the morning. Just... ping. Eyes wide open. The house is dead quiet, my wife is snoring softly next to me, and I'm just lying there in the dark. I'll try to go back to sleep, I'll flip the pillow over to the cool side, try to count backwards from a hundred, all those tricks, but it's no use. I just can't really get back to sleep. I just sort of doze and toss and turn until the alarm finally goes off at five-thirty. 

So, by the time I actually get out of bed and stumble into the kitchen to brew that Folgers I was telling you about, I'm already exhausted. I mean, I still make it to work on time, I'm never late, I take pride in that. But I feel like I'm starting the day already worn down, you know? Like I'm running on a battery that only got charged up to maybe forty percent. It just makes that flat feeling I was talking about even heavier when you're dragging yourself through the day on four hours of bad sleep.

So, I don't really know if I'm *not* enjoying them, it's just... it's just part of the routine now, I guess. Like checking the tire pressure on the rig before a trip. You just do it because it's what you do, not because you get a big kick out of it. Does that make sense?\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you've lost interest in things you used to care about?\n\nPatient: Well, lost interest... see, that's the thing, doc, I don't think I have. Not really. I mean, I still care about doing a good job, you know? Like with my routes. I've been driving this same Freightliner for about six years now, and I still take the time every single morning to make sure she's running right. I check the fluids, I kick the tires, I even wipe down the dash with those Armor All wipes because I can't stand a dusty cab. I wouldn't do all that if I didn't care, right? \n\nAnd it's the same down at the community center. I still care that the bingo night goes off without a hitch. Just last month, Jimmy forgot to order the extra bingo daubers, and I was the one who ran down to the dollar store on Main Street—the one next to the old movie theater—to grab a couple boxes out of my own pocket, because I didn't want the seniors to be disappointed when they showed up. So I definitely still care about things. I still want things to go right. \n\nIt's not like I've just thrown my hands up and said to hell with it all. I've seen guys do that on the road, guys who just let their cabs turn into absolute garbage dumps, fast food wrappers and empty soda bottles everywhere, because they just don't give a damn anymore about anything. But that's not me. I still have an interest in keeping my life in order. I want to make sure my wife is taken care of, make sure the house is in good shape. I've got this whole system with manila folders on the desk in our spare room—one for utilities, one for the mortgage, one for truck maintenance—and I still sit down every single Sunday I'm home to balance it all out and make sure we're in the black. \n\nSo the interest is still there. I still care about all of it, I really do. It's just... well, like I was saying before, it's just that heavy, flat feeling while I'm doing it all. But the caring part? No, I haven't lost that. I'm pretty sure I haven't, anyway.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever feel excited or look forward to anything?\n\nPatient: Excited... look forward to things. Man, that's a tough one. I mean, I guess I don't really get that feeling of, like, counting down the days on the calendar for something, you know? Like, take vacations, for example. My wife and I, usually once a year, we try to go down to her sister's place in Florida. It's nice down there, near Sarasota. We drive down—I prefer driving, obviously, since I do it for a living, and I don't really like the hassle of the airports with the security lines and the tiny seats where my knees are jammed up against the tray table. Plus, taking the truck means we can pack whatever we want. \n\nAnyway, when we're getting ready for that trip, she's always buzzing around the house, making packing lists, talking about which restaurants we're going to hit up, buying new sunscreen or whatever. And I'm just... I'm packing the suitcases into the trunk, checking the oil in her sedan, making sure the tire pressure is good for the highway miles. I'm doing the prep, but I don't have that feeling she has. That buzzing feeling. I'm just looking at it like, 'Okay, next week we will be in Florida instead of here.' \n\nAnd it's the same with the holidays. Thanksgiving, Christmas. We always have the family over, my side and hers, and it's a full house. I do the turkey—I fry it out in the driveway, been doing it that way for ten years since my brother-in-law got me the fryer setup. I get the oil temperature just right, I make sure the bird is completely thawed so it doesn't explode... I do all the steps. But leading up to it, I'm not sitting there thinking, 'Oh boy, I can't wait for Thanksgiving!' It's just another thing on the schedule. \n\nI guess I just don't get that spark of anticipation anymore. I don't dread these things, like I said before. I don't sit there wishing I could just cancel the Florida trip or tell everyone to stay home for Christmas. I'll go, I'll do it, I'll fry the turkey, I'll drive the miles to Sarasota. But that feeling of being excited? Like, really looking forward to it? I just don't think I have that gear anymore. It's just... it's just what happens next on the calendar. So, yeah, I guess I don't really feel excited about much of anything.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever thought about ending your life?\n\nPatient: Ending my life? Lord, no. No, doc. I mean, I get why you have to ask that, I really do. You hear stories, especially in my line of work. Driving long haul, it can get to some guys. You're out there in the cab of the truck, sometimes for days at a time if you're on a bad route, just staring at the asphalt and listening to the hum of those tires, and your mind can go to some pretty dark places if you let it. I knew a guy, a dispatcher out of Omaha about ten years back, who just couldn't take the grind anymore... but that's not me. It's really not. \n\nLike I've been saying, I'm not sitting around in agony or crying my eyes out or feeling like the world is crashing down on me. It's just that flat feeling. I'm just coasting in neutral. And besides, I could never do something like that to my wife. She's put too much time into me, you know? Thirty years we've been married this coming October, and if I just checked out early, it would leave her with an absolute mess. The mortgage, the truck payments, all those manila folders I was telling you about... she hates doing the paperwork. I got the call from my sister while I was pulled over at a rest stop. He had been sick for a bit, it was his heart, so it wasn't a total shock, you know? But still, when it actually happens, it changes things. \n\nI took a couple weeks off work, which I almost never do—I hate leaving my dispatcher hanging—but I had to go help my mom sort out the house and the estate and all that. We had to sell his old Chevy pickup, which honestly broke my heart a little, but she couldn't drive a manual transmission and it was just going to sit there and rust in the driveway. Anyway, we got through the funeral, got the paperwork sorted, and after all the dust settled, I got back in my rig and went back to my routes. \n\nAt first, I figured I was just grieving, you know? Just feeling weighed down because of the funeral and losing the old man. Anyone would feel that way. But then spring turned into summer, and summer into fall, and we had the holidays without him, and that feeling... it just never lifted. It never went away. I kept thinking one morning I'd wake up, brew my coffee, and feel like my old self again—the guy who used to actually whistle while he checked his tire pressure in the morning. But it's been three whole years now of just... coasting. Just that same flat, heavy line every single day since we buried him. So, yeah, I'd say three years is about right.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past three years?\n\nPatient: Weight? No, not really. I mean, you'd think I would have, given the job. You sit behind the wheel of a rig for eleven hours a day, your metabolism isn't exactly doing jumping jacks, you know? And the food out there on the interstate... man, it's a disaster waiting to happen. You pull into a Love's or a Pilot, and it's all roller hot dogs that have been sitting there since the Bush administration, or those fast-food joints where everything is deep-fried. I see guys out there, other drivers, who have just ballooned up. They can barely climb up into the cab without losing their breath, and their knees are shot by the time they're forty-five. \n\nBut my wife, bless her, she tries to keep me in line. She packs this big Coleman cooler for me before I head out on a long haul. Puts in turkey sandwiches, some apples, maybe some of those little carrot sticks. I don't always eat the carrots, if I'm being honest, but I stick to the sandwiches mostly. And when I'm home, my appetite's just... normal, I guess. I eat what she puts in front of me. Pork chops, meatloaf, whatever. I don't really have the drive to go snacking late at night or anything, and I don't skip meals either. Just three meals a day, same as always. \n\nSo, no, the scale hasn't really moved. Has for years. I'm still wearing the same size 36 waist Levi's I was wearing before my dad passed. I just use the exact same notch on my leather belt. So, no, the weight hasn't really fluctuated at all. Just steady. Like everything else, I guess. Just staying exactly the same.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having any problems with your sleep?\n\nPatient: Sleep? Yeah, sleep's... well, it's not great. I mean, it's not like I'm up all night staring at the ceiling fan going round and round, but it's just not what it used to be. You know, back in the day, my head would hit the pillow and I was out cold until the alarm went off. But lately... especially on the nights before a run, it's a whole different story.\n\nI'll get into bed, usually around ten, ten-thirty, right after the late local news—I always like to catch the weather report, you know, just to see what kind of mess I might be driving into the next day—and I'll just lie there. Tired? Well... I mean, like I was just saying with the sleep thing, I definitely feel worn down from that. But as far as just generally lacking energy? I don't know. I'm not really sure I'd call it that. 

I mean, I'm fifty years old, and I drive a truck for a living. So, sure, I'm tired at the end of a shift, but I think anybody would be, you know? It's not like I'm falling asleep at the wheel or anything like that. I keep a big Stanley thermos of coffee with me—just black, no sugar, because sugar gives you that terrible crash later on, which I learned the hard way back in my twenties when I used to drink those giant fountain sodas from the gas station to stay awake. The coffee keeps me going just fine. I still get the job done, I still make my delivery windows. So I don't think I'm completely out of gas or anything. It's probably just... regular tired. Just the wear and tear of the road and getting older, I guess. Nothing out of the ordinary, really.

Moving or speaking more slowly? No... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, my wife always jokes that I talk too much as it is, so if I started slowing down, she'd probably throw a parade just to celebrate the peace and quiet. But seriously, no. You can't really afford to move slow in my line of work, anyway. 

When you're doing a pre-trip inspection on an eighteen-wheeler—which you have to do every single morning, it's strict DOT regulations, you absolutely cannot skip it—you're checking the air brakes, you're thumping the tires to check the pressure, you're looking at the fifth wheel coupling... you're climbing up and down, checking the kingpin, making sure the airlines aren't rubbing. If I was moving like molasses, I'd never get out of the yard on time. And time is money in freight, plain and simple. Dispatch is always breathing down your neck. My dispatcher, this guy Stan, he's a decent enough guy, but he's got a tight schedule to keep, you know? If I was dragging my feet and taking twice as long to get the rig rolling, he'd be blowing up my phone before I even hit the on-ramp for I-80. 

And as for talking... no, I talk just the same as I always have. I still get on the CB radio sometimes, though to be honest it's mostly just quiet these days, not like the old days when everyone was jawing on channel 19. But when I do talk to the guys at the truck stops, or to the receivers at the loading docks, I'm talking at my normal speed. I've always had a bit of a Midwestern pace to my voice, I guess, but I'm not slurring or taking forever to get a sentence out. I just talk like me. Same pace, same everything. So, no, I haven't noticed anything like that. Just the usual.

Like I'm just existing instead of actually living.\n\nDoctor: Do you find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy, like helping out at the community center or spending time with your wife?\n\nPatient: Pleasure... well, doc, I'm not really sure how to answer that, to be honest with you. I get there, I set up the folding chairs—we use those heavy metal ones, you know, because the cheap plastic ones always end up cracking if the older folks lean back too hard—and I talk to Jimmy and the rest of the guys. I wouldn't do all that if I didn't care, right? \n\nAnd it's the same down at the community center. I still care that the bingo night goes off without a hitch. Just last month, Jimmy forgot to order the extra bingo daubers, and I was the one who ran down to the dollar store on Main Street—the one next to the old movie theater—to grab a couple boxes out of my own pocket, because I didn't want the seniors to be disappointed when they showed up. So I definitely still care about things. I still want things to go right. \n\nIt's not like I've just thrown my hands up and said to hell with it all. I've got this whole system with manila folders on the desk in our spare room—one for utilities, one for the mortgage, one for truck maintenance—and I still sit down every single Sunday I'm home to balance it all out and make sure we're in the black. \n\nSo the interest is still there. I still care about all of it, I really do. It's just... well, like I was saying before, it's just that heavy, flat feeling while I'm doing it all. But the caring part? No, I haven't lost that. We always have the family over, my side and hers, and it's a full house. I get the oil temperature just right, I make sure the bird is completely thawed so it doesn't explode... I do all the steps. But leading up to it, I'm not sitting there thinking, 'Oh boy, I can't wait for Thanksgiving!' Concentrating? Well, it's funny you ask that. When I'm actually behind the wheel, out on the open road, that part is almost pure muscle memory by now. I've been shifting those gears and watching those mirrors for so many years, my hands and feet just know what to do without me having to think too hard about it. But... when it comes to the other stuff, the logistics and the paperwork? That's where I've been noticing a little bit of a hiccup lately. 

I mean, I can still do my job, absolutely. I haven't messed up a run or missed a window or anything like that. But lately, I catch myself rereading delivery times on my manifest over and over. Like, I'll be standing in the dispatch office first thing in the morning, looking up at the big dry-erase schedule board that Stan keeps on the wall—he uses all these different colored markers for different regions, red for the local Midwest runs, blue for anything crossing the Mississippi, you get the idea—and I'll just find myself staring at it way longer than I should. I'll look right at my route, see the exact time I'm supposed to drop a load off, and then five minutes later when I'm walking out to the yard to do my pre-trip, I have to pull my clipboard out and check it all over again. 

It's just... it's like my mind doesn't lock onto things the way it used to. I'll read the bill of lading, and my eyes are going over the words, but the actual information just isn't sinking in on the first pass. I'll have to read the same line two or three times just to make sure I'm supposed to be backing into Dock 4 instead of Dock 14. It's frustrating, really, because I used to have a mind like a steel trap for times and numbers. Stan used to just holler a route at me across the room while I was pouring my coffee and I had it memorized for the rest of the day. Now I'm double-checking a piece of paper I just looked at sixty seconds ago. So the driving itself is fine, but getting my brain to actually grip onto those little details... it just feels like the gears are slipping a little bit before they finally catch.

Restless? Or sitting still? No, not really. I mean, I sit still for a living, obviously. You're strapped into that air-ride seat for hours on end, and you literally can't move much even if you wanted to. You've got the steering wheel right there in your chest, the pedals under your feet, and maybe you can shift your weight a little from side to side when your lower back starts barking at you—which it always does after about mile four hundred—but you're pretty much planted. 

But as far as feeling fidgety? No. I don't get the jitters or anything like that. I'm not tapping my foot or drumming my fingers on the dashboard. Honestly, I think if I was a fidgety kind of guy, I would have washed out of trucking decades ago. You see some of these young guys come out of CDL school, and they're all keyed up, bouncing their knees in the driver's lounge, constantly checking their phones, pacing around the fuel islands while they're pumping diesel. They just can't handle the sheer amount of sitting that the job requires. But me? I'm fine with it. I can just sit there, keep my eyes on the horizon, listen to the hum of the tires, and just be still. 

And on the flip side, I don't have times where I just sit and don't *want* to move, either. When it's time to move, I move. When I pull into a truck stop for the night, say the Flying J off I-65 down in Indiana, the first thing I do after I set the parking brakes and log off my electronic logging device is jump out of the cab and stretch my legs. I want to walk around, go inside, get a hot shower, maybe grab a bite at the Denny's if it's not too crowded. I don't just sit in the sleeper berth staring at the wall. So, no, I wouldn't say I have either of those problems. I'm just steady, I guess. I sit when I have to sit, and I move when it's time to move. Nothing unusual there.

She'd be completely lost trying to sort out the utility bills and the insurance premiums, and I take my responsibilities seriously. I always have. \n\nSo, no. I wake up, I brew the coffee—just regular Folgers, I don't mess with that expensive stuff—and I go to work. I'm not looking to end the trip early, I'm just... I'm just not enjoying the scenery as much as I used to, I guess. But checking out? No. Never crossed my mind.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this heavy, flat feeling?\n\nPatient: How long... well, if I really sit down and trace it back, I guess it's been about three years now. Yeah, three years. It started right around the time my dad passed away. \n\nThat was back in, let's see, it would have been early spring. March. I remember it was March because it was still freezing rain up in the panhandle where I was running a load of lumber, and the roads were just a miserable sheet of ice. I got the call from my sister while I was pulled over at a rest stop. He had been sick for a bit, it was his heart, so it wasn't a total shock, you know? But still, when it actually happens, it changes things. \n\nI took a couple weeks off work, which I almost never do—I hate leaving my dispatcher hanging—but I had to go help my mom sort out the house and the estate and all that. We had to sell his old Chevy pickup, which honestly broke my heart a little, but she couldn't drive a manual transmission and it was just going to sit there and rust in the driveway. Anyway, we got through the funeral, got the paperwork sorted, and after all the dust settled, I got back in my rig and went back to my routes. \n\nAt first, I figured I was just grieving, you know? Just feeling weighed down because of the funeral and losing the old man. Anyone would feel that way. But then spring turned into summer, and summer into fall, and we had the holidays without him, and that feeling... it just never lifted. It never went away. I kept thinking one morning I'd wake up, brew my coffee, and feel like my old self again—the guy who used to actually whistle while he checked his tire pressure in the morning. But it's been three whole years now of just... coasting. Just that same flat, heavy line every single day since we buried him. So, yeah, I'd say three years is about right.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past three years?\n\nPatient: Weight? No, not really. I mean, you'd think I would have, given the job. You sit behind the wheel of a rig for eleven hours a day, your metabolism isn't exactly doing jumping jacks, you know? And the food out there on the interstate... man, it's a disaster waiting to happen. You pull into a Love's or a Pilot, and it's all roller hot dogs that have been sitting there since the Bush administration, or those fast-food joints where everything is deep-fried. I see guys out there, other drivers, who have just ballooned up. They can barely climb up into the cab without losing their breath, and their knees are shot by the time they're forty-five. \n\nBut my wife, bless her, she tries to keep me in line. She packs this big Coleman cooler for me before I head out on a long haul. Puts in turkey sandwiches, some apples, maybe some of those little carrot sticks. I don't always eat the carrots, if I'm being honest, but I stick to the sandwiches mostly. And when I'm home, my appetite's just... normal, I guess. I eat what she puts in front of me. Pork chops, meatloaf, whatever. I don't really have the drive to go snacking late at night or anything, and I don't skip meals either. Just three meals a day, same as always. \n\nSo, no, the scale hasn't really moved. I step on it sometimes in the bathroom—it's one of those old analog ones, not the digital kind where the battery always dies when you actually want to use it—and it usually hovers right around 195. Has for years. I'm still wearing the same size 36 waist Levi's I was wearing before my dad passed. I just use the exact same notch on my leather belt. So, no, the weight hasn't really fluctuated at all. Just steady. Like everything else, I guess. Just staying exactly the same.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having any problems with your sleep?\n\nPatient: Sleep? Yeah, sleep's... well, it's not great. I mean, it's not like I'm up all night staring at the ceiling fan going round and round, but it's just not what it used to be. You know, back in the day, my head would hit the pillow and I was out cold until the alarm went off. My wife used to joke that a freight train could drive right through the bedroom and I wouldn't even flinch. But lately... especially on the nights before a run, it's a whole different story.\n\nI'll get into bed, usually around ten, ten-thirty, right after the late local news—I always like to catch the weather report, you know, just to see what kind of mess I might be driving into the next day—and I'll just lie there. I'll be trying to shut my brain off, but instead, I'm just running through the whole route in my head. I'll be thinking about the next day's stops, worrying if the loading dock at the warehouse in Des Moines is going to be backed up again, or if I need to take the bypass around Chicago because of that construction on 94... just all these little details that I shouldn't be sweating at eleven o'clock at night. \n\nAnd then, even when I do finally drift off, it's not a deep sleep. It's that light, choppy kind of sleep where you feel like you're half awake the whole time. And then, without fail, I'll wake up around four in the morning. Just... ping. Eyes wide open. The house is dead quiet, my wife is snoring softly next to me, and I'm just lying there in the dark. I'll try to go back to sleep, I'll flip the pillow over to the cool side, try to count backwards from a hundred, all those tricks, but it's no use. I just can't really get back to sleep. I just sort of doze and toss and turn until the alarm finally goes off at five-thirty. \n\nSo, by the time I actually get out of bed and stumble into the kitchen to brew that Folgers I was telling you about, I'm already exhausted. I mean, I still make it to work on time, I'm never late, I take pride in that. But I feel like I'm starting the day already worn down, you know? Like I'm running on a battery that only got charged up to maybe forty percent. It just makes that flat feeling I was talking about even heavier when you're dragging yourself through the day on four hours of bad sleep.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel tired or lacking in energy?\n\nPatient: Tired? Well... I mean, like I was just saying with the sleep thing, I definitely feel worn down from that. But as far as just generally lacking energy? I don't know. I'm not really sure I'd call it that. \n\nI mean, I'm fifty years old, and I drive a truck for a living. You sit in that cab for ten, eleven hours, staring at the white lines on the interstate, feeling the rumble of that big diesel engine right up through the floorboards... it kind of vibrates right into your bones after a few hundred miles. It takes it out of you. And sometimes, depending on the contract, I have to help unload. Like just last week, I was hauling a load of heavy-duty tractor parts down to Peoria, and the forklift operator at the receiving dock was on his lunch break. So I had to get back there in the trailer and start moving pallets around myself with a manual hand jack. By the time I was done, my shoulders were absolutely burning. \n\nSo, sure, I'm tired at the end of a shift, but I think anybody would be, you know? It's not like I'm falling asleep at the wheel or anything like that. I keep a big Stanley thermos of coffee with me—just black, no sugar, because sugar gives you that terrible crash later on, which I learned the hard way back in my twenties when I used to drink those giant fountain sodas from the gas station to stay awake. The coffee keeps me going just fine. I still get the job done, I still make my delivery windows. So I don't think I'm completely out of gas or anything. It's probably just... regular tired. Just the wear and tear of the road and getting older, I guess. Nothing out of the ordinary, really.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself moving or speaking more slowly than you used to?\n\nPatient: Moving or speaking more slowly? No... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, my wife always jokes that I talk too much as it is, so if I started slowing down, she'd probably throw a parade just to celebrate the peace and quiet. But seriously, no. You can't really afford to move slow in my line of work, anyway. \n\nWhen you're doing a pre-trip inspection on an eighteen-wheeler—which you have to do every single morning, it's strict DOT regulations, you absolutely cannot skip it—you're checking the air brakes, you're thumping the tires to check the pressure, you're looking at the fifth wheel coupling... you're climbing up and down, checking the kingpin, making sure the airlines aren't rubbing. If I was moving like molasses, I'd never get out of the yard on time. And time is money in freight, plain and simple. Dispatch is always breathing down your neck. My dispatcher, this guy Stan, he's a decent enough guy, but he's got a tight schedule to keep, you know? If I was dragging my feet and taking twice as long to get the rig rolling, he'd be blowing up my phone before I even hit the on-ramp for I-80. \n\nAnd as for talking... no, I talk just the same as I always have. I still get on the CB radio sometimes, though to be honest it's mostly just quiet these days, not like the old days when everyone was jawing on channel 19. But when I do talk to the guys at the truck stops, or to the receivers at the loading docks, I'm talking at my normal speed. I've always had a bit of a Midwestern pace to my voice, I guess, but I'm not slurring or taking forever to get a sentence out. I just talk like me. Same pace, same everything. So, no, I haven't noticed anything like that. Just the usual.\n\nDoctor: Do you have trouble concentrating on tasks, like when you're driving or helping at the community center?\n\nPatient: Concentrating? Well, it's funny you ask that. When I'm actually behind the wheel, out on the open road, that part is almost pure muscle memory by now. I've been shifting those gears and watching those mirrors for so many years, my hands and feet just know what to do without me having to think too hard about it. But... when it comes to the other stuff, the logistics and the paperwork? That's where I've been noticing a little bit of a hiccup lately. \n\nI mean, I can still do my job, absolutely. I haven't messed up a run or missed a window or anything like that. But lately, I catch myself rereading delivery times on my manifest over and over. Like, I'll be standing in the dispatch office first thing in the morning, looking up at the big dry-erase schedule board that Stan keeps on the wall—he uses all these different colored markers for different regions, red for the local Midwest runs, blue for anything crossing the Mississippi, you get the idea—and I'll just find myself staring at it way longer than I should. I'll look right at my route, see the exact time I'm supposed to drop a load off, and then five minutes later when I'm walking out to the yard to do my pre-trip, I have to pull my clipboard out and check it all over again. \n\nIt's just... it's like my mind doesn't lock onto things the way it used to. I'll read the bill of lading, and my eyes are going over the words, but the actual information just isn't sinking in on the first pass. I'll have to read the same line two or three times just to make sure I'm supposed to be backing into Dock 4 instead of Dock 14. It's frustrating, really, because I used to have a mind like a steel trap for times and numbers. Stan used to just holler a route at me across the room while I was pouring my coffee and I had it memorized for the rest of the day. Now I'm double-checking a piece of paper I just looked at sixty seconds ago. So the driving itself is fine, but getting my brain to actually grip onto those little details... it just feels like the gears are slipping a little bit before they finally catch.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself feeling restless or fidgety, or do you have periods where you just sit still and don't want to move?\n\nPatient: Restless? Or sitting still? No, not really. I mean, I sit still for a living, obviously. You're strapped into that air-ride seat for hours on end, and you literally can't move much even if you wanted to. You've got the steering wheel right there in your chest, the pedals under your feet, and maybe you can shift your weight a little from side to side when your lower back starts barking at you—which it always does after about mile four hundred—but you're pretty much planted. \n\nBut as far as feeling fidgety? No. I don't get the jitters or anything like that. I'm not tapping my foot or drumming my fingers on the dashboard. Honestly, I think if I was a fidgety kind of guy, I would have washed out of trucking decades ago. You see some of these young guys come out of CDL school, and they're all keyed up, bouncing their knees in the driver's lounge, constantly checking their phones, pacing around the fuel islands while they're pumping diesel. They just can't handle the sheer amount of sitting that the job requires. But me? I'm fine with it. I can just sit there, keep my eyes on the horizon, listen to the hum of the tires, and just be still. \n\nAnd on the flip side, I don't have times where I just sit and don't *want* to move, either. When it's time to move, I move. When I pull into a truck stop for the night, say the Flying J off I-65 down in Indiana, the first thing I do after I set the parking brakes and log off my electronic logging device is jump out of the cab and stretch my legs. I want to walk around, go inside, get a hot shower, maybe grab a bite at the Denny's if it's not too crowded. I don't just sit in the sleeper berth staring at the wall. Guilty? Hmm. Well... no, I wouldn't say I sit around feeling guilty. I mean, you know, when you drive a truck for a living, you do miss things. That's just the nature of the beast. Hopeless? No, I wouldn't use a word like that. I mean, if you listen to the CB radio these days—which, honestly, I keep turned off half the time now because it's just a bunch of guys griping—you'd think the sky was falling. It's not hopeless. It's just predictable, I guess.

It takes a lot of the actual art out of driving. You feel more like a steering wheel attendant than a real truck driver sometimes. 

But just because things change or get a little more corporate doesn't mean the future is doomed, you know? It just means it's different. I don't get that feeling of doom and gloom that some guys get. I just wake up, pour my coffee in my thermos, go out to the yard, check my oil, thump my tires, and put it in gear. Tomorrow is just another page in the logbook. It might not be the most exciting future in the world, but it's certainly not hopeless. It's just the road ahead.

I still get on the CB radio sometimes, though to be honest it's mostly just quiet these days, not like the old days when everyone was jawing on channel 19. But when I do talk to the guys at the truck stops, or to the receivers at the loading docks, I'm talking at my normal speed. I've always had a bit of a Midwestern pace to my voice, I guess, but I'm not slurring or taking forever to get a sentence out. I just talk like me. Same pace, same everything. So, no, I haven't noticed anything like that. Just the usual.\n\nDoctor: Do you have trouble concentrating on tasks, like when you're driving or helping at the community center?\n\nPatient: Concentrating? Well, it's funny you ask that. When I'm actually behind the wheel, out on the open road, that part is almost pure muscle memory by now. I've been shifting those gears and watching those mirrors for so many years, my hands and feet just know what to do without me having to think too hard about it. But... when it comes to the other stuff, the logistics and the paperwork? That's where I've been noticing a little bit of a hiccup lately. \n\nI mean, I can still do my job, absolutely. I haven't messed up a run or missed a window or anything like that. But lately, I catch myself rereading delivery times on my manifest over and over. Like, I'll be standing in the dispatch office first thing in the morning, looking up at the big dry-erase schedule board that Stan keeps on the wall—he uses all these different colored markers for different regions, red for the local Midwest runs, blue for anything crossing the Mississippi, you get the idea—and I'll just find myself staring at it way longer than I should. I'll look right at my route, see the exact time I'm supposed to drop a load off, and then five minutes later when I'm walking out to the yard to do my pre-trip, I have to pull my clipboard out and check it all over again. \n\nIt's just... it's like my mind doesn't lock onto things the way it used to. I'll read the bill of lading, and my eyes are going over the words, but the actual information just isn't sinking in on the first pass. I'll have to read the same line two or three times just to make sure I'm supposed to be backing into Dock 4 instead of Dock 14. It's frustrating, really, because I used to have a mind like a steel trap for times and numbers. Stan used to just holler a route at me across the room while I was pouring my coffee and I had it memorized for the rest of the day. Now I'm double-checking a piece of paper I just looked at sixty seconds ago. So the driving itself is fine, but getting my brain to actually grip onto those little details... it just feels like the gears are slipping a little bit before they finally catch.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself feeling restless or fidgety, or do you have periods where you just sit still and don't want to move?\n\nPatient: Restless? Or sitting still? No, not really. I mean, I sit still for a living, obviously. You're strapped into that air-ride seat for hours on end, and you literally can't move much even if you wanted to. You've got the steering wheel right there in your chest, the pedals under your feet, and maybe you can shift your weight a little from side to side when your lower back starts barking at you—which it always does after about mile four hundred—but you're pretty much planted. \n\nBut as far as feeling fidgety? No. I don't get the jitters or anything like that. I'm not tapping my foot or drumming my fingers on the dashboard. Honestly, I think if I was a fidgety kind of guy, I would have washed out of trucking decades ago. You see some of these young guys come out of CDL school, and they're all keyed up, bouncing their knees in the driver's lounge, constantly checking their phones, pacing around the fuel islands while they're pumping diesel. They just can't handle the sheer amount of sitting that the job requires. But me? I'm fine with it. I can just sit there, keep my eyes on the horizon, listen to the hum of the tires, and just be still. \n\nAnd on the flip side, I don't have times where I just sit and don't *want* to move, either. When it's time to move, I move. When I pull into a truck stop for the night, say the Flying J off I-65 down in Indiana, the first thing I do after I set the parking brakes and log off my electronic logging device is jump out of the cab and stretch my legs. I want to walk around, go inside, get a hot shower, maybe grab a bite at the Denny's if it's not too crowded. I don't just sit in the sleeper berth staring at the wall. So, no, I wouldn't say I have either of those problems. I'm just steady, I guess. I sit when I have to sit, and I move when it's time to move. Nothing unusual there.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel guilty about things that have happened in your life?\n\nPatient: Guilty? Hmm. Well... no, I wouldn't say I sit around feeling guilty. I mean, you know, when you drive a truck for a living, you do miss things. That's just the nature of the beast. You're out on the road for weeks at a time sometimes, especially back when I was doing long-haul, over-the-road stuff before I got a slightly better dedicated route. And you see guys out there at the truck stops, sitting at the diner counters, staring at their coffee cups, just eating themselves alive with guilt because they missed their kid's high school graduation, or they weren't there for their wife's birthday because they were stuck in a white-out blizzard on Donner Pass. \n\nBut me? I never really let that stuff get to me in that way. I mean, my wife and I, we had an understanding from day one. She knew what she was signing up for when she married a trucker. I remember this one time, it was our tenth anniversary, and I was supposed to be home by Friday night. I had this whole plan to take her to this nice steakhouse down by the river. But then my rig threw a belt right outside of Omaha, and I was stranded on the shoulder of I-80 for six hours waiting for a road service guy because dispatch couldn't get anyone out there any faster. By the time I got rolling again, there was no way I was making it back. I ended up eating a microwaved burrito at a Love's Travel Stop at midnight. \n\nNow, some guys would beat themselves up over that for years. They'd feel so guilty they couldn't sleep. I try to treat people right, do my job, and get the freight where it needs to go. So, no... I don't really have that guilt weighing me down. I just kind of take life as it comes, bump by bump.\n\nDoctor: Do you often think that the future seems hopeless or that things will never get better?\n\nPatient: Hopeless? It takes a lot of the actual art out of driving. Self-harm? No. Lord, no. I mean, don't get me wrong, when the old man passed... that was a heavy load to haul. I was actually down near Macon, Georgia, pulling a reefer trailer full of frozen chicken, when my sister called me with the news. I had to pull over at this little dirt-lot rest area just to process it. And you know, you're sitting there in the cab, the diesel's idling, the refrigeration unit on the trailer is kicking on and off, vibrating the whole rig, and you just feel... empty. 

He was the one who actually taught me how to drive, you know? Started me out on an old farm tractor when I was barely tall enough to reach the clutch, then moved me up to a straight truck hauling feed. So losing him... yeah, it hit me hard. Really hard. I'm not gonna sit here and pretend it didn't take the wind right out of my sails for a good long while. I felt pretty low. 

But hurting myself? No. No, that never crossed my mind. That's just... that's not how I'm wired, and honestly, he would have come back from the grave and kicked my behind if I ever even entertained a thought like that. You get a lot of windshield time out on the interstate, a lot of hours in the dark with just the headlights cutting through the night, and your mind definitely wanders. You think about the past, you think about the folks who aren't around anymore. I shed more than a few tears gripping that steering wheel those first few months, I'll be the first to admit that. 

But wanting to end it? Thinking about steering the rig into a bridge abutment or something crazy like that? Never. Well, let's see... if I look back at the logbook of my life, so to speak, I'd say it's been right about three years now. Yeah, three years this past fall. It all really settled in right after my father died. Like I was telling you before, about being down in Georgia with that load of frozen chicken when I got the call... ever since that day, it's just been this steady, unchanging feeling. 

You asked if there are periods where I feel better, and, well... I wouldn't say I have these big highs and lows. It's not like driving a mountain pass out in Colorado where you're grinding your way up to the summit in low gear and then flying down the other side. It's more like... well, like I said earlier about the Texas panhandle. Just flat. For three whole years. 

I kept thinking, you know, maybe after the first anniversary of his death, things would pick up. People tell you that all the time. They say, "Oh, the first holidays are the hardest, the first Thanksgiving, the first Christmas without him." And my wife, bless her heart, she really tried to make that first Christmas special. She made his favorite pecan pie, we got a bigger tree for the living room... but I just sat there in my armchair, looking at the lights, and I just felt... exactly the same. Flat. 

And then the second year rolled around, and the third, and I was out on the road, hauling freight up through the Midwest or down the Eastern seaboard, and I realized, huh, this feeling hasn't really lifted. It hasn't gotten worse, mind you. I'm still doing my job, still doing my pre-trip inspections, still paying the mortgage on time, but it hasn't gotten any better either. It's just been this constant, steady, low hum... kind of like the sound of a diesel engine idling when you're trying to sleep in the sleeper berth at a rest stop. You get used to it, you can function with it, but you're always aware that it's there, just humming away in the background. So, yeah, three years of just... this. Just a long, flat stretch of road since he passed.

It's really not. \n\nLike I've been saying, I'm not sitting around in agony or crying my eyes out or feeling like the world is crashing down on me. It's just that flat feeling. I'm just coasting in neutral. And besides, I could never do something like that to my wife. She's put too much time into me, you know? Thirty years we've been married this coming October, and if I just checked out early, it would leave her with an absolute mess. The mortgage, the truck payments, all those manila folders I was telling you about... she hates doing the paperwork. She'd be completely lost trying to sort out the utility bills and the insurance premiums, and I take my responsibilities seriously. I always have. \n\nSo, no. I wake up, I brew the coffee—just regular Folgers, I don't mess with that expensive stuff—and I go to work. I'm not looking to end the trip early, I'm just... I'm just not enjoying the scenery as much as I used to, I guess. But checking out? No. Never crossed my mind.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this heavy, flat feeling?\n\nPatient: How long... well, if I really sit down and trace it back, I guess it's been about three years now. Yeah, three years. It started right around the time my dad passed away. \n\nThat was back in, let's see, it would have been early spring. March. I remember it was March because it was still freezing rain up in the panhandle where I was running a load of lumber, and the roads were just a miserable sheet of ice. I got the call from my sister while I was pulled over at a rest stop. He had been sick for a bit, it was his heart, so it wasn't a total shock, you know? But still, when it actually happens, it changes things. \n\nI took a couple weeks off work, which I almost never do—I hate leaving my dispatcher hanging—but I had to go help my mom sort out the house and the estate and all that. We had to sell his old Chevy pickup, which honestly broke my heart a little, but she couldn't drive a manual transmission and it was just going to sit there and rust in the driveway. Anyway, we got through the funeral, got the paperwork sorted, and after all the dust settled, I got back in my rig and went back to my routes. \n\nAt first, I figured I was just grieving, you know? Just feeling weighed down because of the funeral and losing the old man. Anyone would feel that way. But then spring turned into summer, and summer into fall, and we had the holidays without him, and that feeling... it just never lifted. It never went away. I kept thinking one morning I'd wake up, brew my coffee, and feel like my old self again—the guy who used to actually whistle while he checked his tire pressure in the morning. But it's been three whole years now of just... coasting. Just that same flat, heavy line every single day since we buried him. So, yeah, I'd say three years is about right.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past three years?\n\nPatient: Weight? No, not really. I mean, you'd think I would have, given the job. You sit behind the wheel of a rig for eleven hours a day, your metabolism isn't exactly doing jumping jacks, you know? And the food out there on the interstate... man, it's a disaster waiting to happen. You pull into a Love's or a Pilot, and it's all roller hot dogs that have been sitting there since the Bush administration, or those fast-food joints where everything is deep-fried. I see guys out there, other drivers, who have just ballooned up. They can barely climb up into the cab without losing their breath, and their knees are shot by the time they're forty-five. \n\nBut my wife, bless her, she tries to keep me in line. I don't always eat the carrots, if I'm being honest, but I stick to the sandwiches mostly. And when I'm home, my appetite's just... normal, I guess. I eat what she puts in front of me. Pork chops, meatloaf, whatever. I don't really have the drive to go snacking late at night or anything, and I don't skip meals either. Just three meals a day, same as always. \n\nSo, no, the scale hasn't really moved. I step on it sometimes in the bathroom—it's one of those old analog ones, not the digital kind where the battery always dies when you actually want to use it—and it usually hovers right around 195. Has for years. I'm still wearing the same size 36 waist Levi's I was wearing before my dad passed. I just use the exact same notch on my leather belt. So, no, the weight hasn't really fluctuated at all. Just steady. Like everything else, I guess. Just staying exactly the same.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having any problems with your sleep?\n\nPatient: Sleep? Yeah, sleep's... well, it's not great. I mean, it's not like I'm up all night staring at the ceiling fan going round and round, but it's just not what it used to be. You know, back in the day, my head would hit the pillow and I was out cold until the alarm went off. I'll be trying to shut my brain off, but instead, I'm just running through the whole route in my head. I'll be thinking about the next day's stops, worrying if the loading dock at the warehouse in Des Moines is going to be backed up again, or if I need to take the bypass around Chicago because of that construction on 94... just all these little details that I shouldn't be sweating at eleven o'clock at night. \n\nAnd then, even when I do finally drift off, it's not a deep sleep. It's that light, choppy kind of sleep where you feel like you're half awake the whole time. And then, without fail, I'll wake up around four in the morning. Just... ping. Eyes wide open. The house is dead quiet, my wife is snoring softly next to me, and I'm just lying there in the dark. I'll try to go back to sleep, I'll flip the pillow over to the cool side, try to count backwards from a hundred, all those tricks, but it's no use. I just can't really get back to sleep. I just sort of doze and toss and turn until the alarm finally goes off at five-thirty. \n\nSo, by the time I actually get out of bed and stumble into the kitchen to brew that Folgers I was telling you about, I'm already exhausted. Just staying exactly the same.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having any problems with your sleep?\n\nPatient: Sleep? Yeah, sleep's... well, it's not great. I mean, it's not like I'm up all night staring at the ceiling fan going round and round, but it's just not what it used to be. You know, back in the day, my head would hit the pillow and I was out cold until the alarm went off. My wife used to joke that a freight train could drive right through the bedroom and I wouldn't even flinch. But lately... especially on the nights before a run, it's a whole different story.\n\nI'll get into bed, usually around ten, ten-thirty, right after the late local news—I always like to catch the weather report, you know, just to see what kind of mess I might be driving into the next day—and I'll just lie there. I'll be trying to shut my brain off, but instead, I'm just running through the whole route in my head. I'll be thinking about the next day's stops, worrying if the loading dock at the warehouse in Des Moines is going to be backed up again, or if I need to take the bypass around Chicago because of that construction on 94... just all these little details that I shouldn't be sweating at eleven o'clock at night. \n\nAnd then, even when I do finally drift off, it's not a deep sleep. It's that light, choppy kind of sleep where you feel like you're half awake the whole time. And then, without fail, I'll wake up around four in the morning. Just... ping. Eyes wide open. The house is dead quiet, my wife is snoring softly next to me, and I'm just lying there in the dark. I'll try to go back to sleep, I'll flip the pillow over to the cool side, try to count backwards from a hundred, all those tricks, but it's no use. I just can't really get back to sleep. I just sort of doze and toss and turn until the alarm finally goes off at five-thirty. \n\nSo, by the time I actually get out of bed and stumble into the kitchen to brew that Folgers I was telling you about, I'm already exhausted. I mean, I still make it to work on time, I'm never late, I take pride in that. But I feel like I'm starting the day already worn down, you know? Like I'm running on a battery that only got charged up to maybe forty percent. It just makes that flat feeling I was talking about even heavier when you're dragging yourself through the day on four hours of bad sleep.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel tired or lacking in energy?\n\nPatient: Tired? Well... I mean, like I was just saying with the sleep thing, I definitely feel worn down from that. But as far as just generally lacking energy? I don't know. I'm not really sure I'd call it that. \n\nI mean, I'm fifty years old, and I drive a truck for a living. You sit in that cab for ten, eleven hours, staring at the white lines on the interstate, feeling the rumble of that big diesel engine right up through the floorboards... it kind of vibrates right into your bones after a few hundred miles. It takes it out of you. And sometimes, depending on the contract, I have to help unload. Like just last week, I was hauling a load of heavy-duty tractor parts down to Peoria, and the forklift operator at the receiving dock was on his lunch break. So I had to get back there in the trailer and start moving pallets around myself with a manual hand jack. By the time I was done, my shoulders were absolutely burning. \n\nSo, sure, I'm tired at the end of a shift, but I think anybody would be, you know? It's not like I'm falling asleep at the wheel or anything like that. I keep a big Stanley thermos of coffee with me—just black, no sugar, because sugar gives you that terrible crash later on, which I learned the hard way back in my twenties when I used to drink those giant fountain sodas from the gas station to stay awake. The coffee keeps me going just fine. I still get the job done, I still make my delivery windows. So I don't think I'm completely out of gas or anything. It's probably just... regular tired. Just the wear and tear of the road and getting older, I guess. Nothing out of the ordinary, really.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself moving or speaking more slowly than you used to?\n\nPatient: Moving or speaking more slowly? No... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, my wife always jokes that I talk too much as it is, so if I started slowing down, she'd probably throw a parade just to celebrate the peace and quiet. But seriously, no. You can't really afford to move slow in my line of work, anyway. \n\nWhen you're doing a pre-trip inspection on an eighteen-wheeler—which you have to do every single morning, it's strict DOT regulations, you absolutely cannot skip it—you're checking the air brakes, you're thumping the tires to check the pressure, you're looking at the fifth wheel coupling... you're climbing up and down, checking the kingpin, making sure the airlines aren't rubbing. If I was moving like molasses, I'd never get out of the yard on time. And time is money in freight, plain and simple. Dispatch is always breathing down your neck. My dispatcher, this guy Stan, he's a decent enough guy, but he's got a tight schedule to keep, you know? If I was dragging my feet and taking twice as long to get the rig rolling, he'd be blowing up my phone before I even hit the on-ramp for I-80. \n\nAnd as for talking... no, I talk just the same as I always have. I still get on the CB radio sometimes, though to be honest it's mostly just quiet these days, not like the old days when everyone was jawing on channel 19. But when I do talk to the guys at the truck stops, or to the receivers at the loading docks, I'm talking at my normal speed. I've always had a bit of a Midwestern pace to my voice, I guess, but I'm not slurring or taking forever to get a sentence out. I just talk like me. Same pace, same everything. So, no, I haven't noticed anything like that. Just the usual.\n\nDoctor: Do you have trouble concentrating on tasks, like when you're driving or helping at the community center?\n\nPatient: Concentrating? Well, it's funny you ask that. When I'm actually behind the wheel, out on the open road, that part is almost pure muscle memory by now. I've been shifting those gears and watching those mirrors for so many years, my hands and feet just know what to do without me having to think too hard about it. But... when it comes to the other stuff, the logistics and the paperwork? That's where I've been noticing a little bit of a hiccup lately. \n\nI mean, I can still do my job, absolutely. I haven't messed up a run or missed a window or anything like that. But lately, I catch myself rereading delivery times on my manifest over and over. Like, I'll be standing in the dispatch office first thing in the morning, looking up at the big dry-erase schedule board that Stan keeps on the wall—he uses all these different colored markers for different regions, red for the local Midwest runs, blue for anything crossing the Mississippi, you get the idea—and I'll just find myself staring at it way longer than I should. I'll look right at my route, see the exact time I'm supposed to drop a load off, and then five minutes later when I'm walking out to the yard to do my pre-trip, I have to pull my clipboard out and check it all over again. \n\nIt's just... it's like my mind doesn't lock onto things the way it used to. I'll read the bill of lading, and my eyes are going over the words, but the actual information just isn't sinking in on the first pass. I'll have to read the same line two or three times just to make sure I'm supposed to be backing into Dock 4 instead of Dock 14. It's frustrating, really, because I used to have a mind like a steel trap for times and numbers. Stan used to just holler a route at me across the room while I was pouring my coffee and I had it memorized for the rest of the day. Now I'm double-checking a piece of paper I just looked at sixty seconds ago. So the driving itself is fine, but getting my brain to actually grip onto those little details... it just feels like the gears are slipping a little bit before they finally catch.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself feeling restless or fidgety, or do you have periods where you just sit still and don't want to move?\n\nPatient: Restless? Or sitting still? No, not really. I mean, I sit still for a living, obviously. You're strapped into that air-ride seat for hours on end, and you literally can't move much even if you wanted to. You've got the steering wheel right there in your chest, the pedals under your feet, and maybe you can shift your weight a little from side to side when your lower back starts barking at you—which it always does after about mile four hundred—but you're pretty much planted. \n\nBut as far as feeling fidgety? No. I don't get the jitters or anything like that. I'm not tapping my foot or drumming my fingers on the dashboard. Honestly, I think if I was a fidgety kind of guy, I would have washed out of trucking decades ago. You see some of these young guys come out of CDL school, and they're all keyed up, bouncing their knees in the driver's lounge, constantly checking their phones, pacing around the fuel islands while they're pumping diesel. They just can't handle the sheer amount of sitting that the job requires. But me? I'm fine with it. I can just sit there, keep my eyes on the horizon, listen to the hum of the tires, and just be still. \n\nAnd on the flip side, I don't have times where I just sit and don't *want* to move, either. When it's time to move, I move. When I pull into a truck stop for the night, say the Flying J off I-65 down in Indiana, the first thing I do after I set the parking brakes and log off my electronic logging device is jump out of the cab and stretch my legs. I want to walk around, go inside, get a hot shower, maybe grab a bite at the Denny's if it's not too crowded. I don't just sit in the sleeper berth staring at the wall. So, no, I wouldn't say I have either of those problems. I'm just steady, I guess. I sit when I have to sit, and I move when it's time to move. Nothing unusual there.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel guilty about things that have happened in your life?\n\nPatient: Guilty? Hmm. Well... no, I wouldn't say I sit around feeling guilty. I mean, you know, when you drive a truck for a living, you do miss things. That's just the nature of the beast. You're out on the road for weeks at a time sometimes, especially back when I was doing long-haul, over-the-road stuff before I got a slightly better dedicated route. And you see guys out there at the truck stops, sitting at the diner counters, staring at their coffee cups, just eating themselves alive with guilt because they missed their kid's high school graduation, or they weren't there for their wife's birthday because they were stuck in a white-out blizzard on Donner Pass. \n\nBut me? I never really let that stuff get to me in that way. I mean, my wife and I, we had an understanding from day one. She knew what she was signing up for when she married a trucker. I remember this one time, it was our tenth anniversary, and I was supposed to be home by Friday night. I had this whole plan to take her to this nice steakhouse down by the river. By the time I got rolling again, there was no way I was making it back. I ended up eating a microwaved burrito at a Love's Travel Stop at midnight. \n\nNow, some guys would beat themselves up over that for years. They'd feel so guilty they couldn't sleep. But I just called her up, explained what happened, and we celebrated on Tuesday instead. You just do the best you can, you know? I've always worked hard, I've always provided, and I've always kept my nose clean. I don't have any dark secrets or terrible mistakes hanging over my head. I try to treat people right, do my job, and get the freight where it needs to go. So, no... I don't really have that guilt weighing me down. I just kind of take life as it comes, bump by bump.\n\nDoctor: Do you often think that the future seems hopeless or that things will never get better?\n\nPatient: Hopeless? No, I wouldn't use a word like that. I mean, if you listen to the CB radio these days—which, honestly, I keep turned off half the time now because it's just a bunch of guys griping—you'd think the sky was falling. Used to be you could get good bear reports or find out which scale houses were open, but now it's just endless complaining about freight rates and fuel prices and the new regulations. But me? I don't look at the future and see some big black hole or anything. \n\nI kind of just look at the future like... well, like a long stretch of I-40 out in the Texas panhandle. You know it's going to be a long ride, and you know the scenery is going to look pretty much exactly the same for the next four or five hundred miles—just flat dirt, sagebrush, and mile markers ticking by—but you also know you're going to get to Amarillo eventually. It's not hopeless. It's just predictable, I guess. \n\nI don't sit in the cab thinking things will never get better, because things aren't really all that bad to begin with. They're just kind of... flat. Steady. Like I said, I've got my dedicated route, my wife and I are doing fine, the mortgage is mostly paid down. You feel more like a steering wheel attendant than a real truck driver sometimes. \n\nBut just because things change or get a little more corporate doesn't mean the future is doomed, you know? It just means it's different. I don't get that feeling of doom and gloom that some guys get. I just wake up, pour my coffee in my thermos, go out to the yard, check my oil, thump my tires, and put it in gear. Tomorrow is just another page in the logbook. It might not be the most exciting future in the world, but it's certainly not hopeless. It's just the road ahead.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any thoughts of self-harm or suicidal ideation since your father passed away?\n\nPatient: Self-harm? No. Lord, no. That's just... that's not how I'm wired, and honestly, he would have come back from the grave and kicked my behind if I ever even entertained a thought like that. You get a lot of windshield time out on the interstate, a lot of hours in the dark with just the headlights cutting through the night, and your mind definitely wanders. You think about the past, you think about the folks who aren't around anymore. Thinking about steering the rig into a bridge abutment or something crazy like that? Never. I've got my wife to get home to, I've got a house to maintain, and I've got a job to do. When you lose somebody, you just... you just keep the wheels turning, you know? You put it in gear and you keep moving forward because that's all you really can do. So, no, I haven't had any thoughts like that at all. Not even close.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this way, and has it been constant or have you had periods where you felt better?\n\nPatient: Well, let's see... if I look back at the logbook of my life, so to speak, I'd say it's been right about three years now. Yeah, three years this past fall. It all really settled in right after my father died. Like I was telling you before, about being down in Georgia with that load of frozen chicken when I got the call... ever since that day, it's just been this steady, unchanging feeling. \n\nYou asked if there are periods where I feel better, and, well... It's more like... well, like I said earlier about the Texas panhandle. Just flat. She made his favorite pecan pie, we got a bigger tree for the living room... but I just sat there in my armchair, looking at the lights, and I just felt... exactly the same. Flat. \n\nAnd then the second year rolled around, and the third, and I was out on the road, hauling freight up through the Midwest or down the Eastern seaboard, and I realized, huh, this feeling hasn't really lifted. It's just been this constant, steady, low hum... kind of like the sound of a diesel engine idling when you're trying to sleep in the sleeper berth at a rest stop. You get used to it, you can function with it, but you're always aware that it's there, just humming away in the background. So, yeah, three years of just... this. Just a long, flat stretch of road since he passed.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself moving or speaking more slowly than you used to, or do you feel like you're speeding up and can't slow down?\n\nPatient: Moving slower? Or speeding up? No... no, I wouldn't say either of those. I mean, look, I'm fifty years old now, so I'm not exactly springing up into the cab like a jackrabbit the way I did when I was twenty-five and fresh out of CDL school, but I'm certainly not moving through molasses either. You know, you just get into a rhythm with this job. A steady pace. Like when I do my pre-trip inspection every morning out in the yard. I've got my routine, right? Well, unable to experience pleasure... that's a tricky one to answer, Doc. Because it's not like I don't enjoy anything at all anymore. It's more like... well, let me explain it like this. You take my old Ford pickup, right? A '78 F-150, cherry red, absolute beauty. I used to spend hours out in the driveway on a Sunday afternoon, polishing that chrome bumper until you could see your reflection in it clear as day. I'd have the radio on, listening to the ballgame, maybe sipping on a cold iced tea my wife brought out for me. And I loved it. I really did. It felt good to see that truck shine, knowing I put the elbow grease into it. 

Now? Well, I still wash the truck. I still get the bucket out, mix up the soap, get the sponge, and go over the whole thing. I don't let it sit there and rust or get covered in pollen and road grime. But when I'm out there doing it... it's just a chore now. I don't get that same kick out of it. I'm just going through the motions, you know? Just scrubbing the hood because the hood needs scrubbing, not because I'm looking forward to seeing it gleam in the sun. 

And it's not just the truck, either. My wife and I, we used to love going to this little diner out on Route 9 on Friday nights. They make this meatloaf that's just out of this world, with real mashed potatoes, not the instant stuff. We'd sit in our favorite booth by the window, watch the cars go by, and just enjoy a good meal after a long week on the road. We still go, mostly because she likes it, and I'm not gonna sit home and stare at the wall while she eats alone. But the meatloaf... it just tastes like food now. It fills the tank, so to speak, but I don't savor it the way I used to. 

So, it's not that I can't do the things I used to enjoy, or that I've completely stopped doing them. I haven't locked myself in a dark room or anything drastic like that. I still go to the diner, I still wash the truck, I still watch the football games on Sunday. But the spark... that little bit of joy that used to come with those things... it's just sort of fizzled out. It's like listening to the radio when you're driving through a valley and the signal gets all fuzzy. You can still hear the song, you know the words, but the music just doesn't sound as good as it did when you had a clear signal. That's kind of how everything feels right now. Just... fuzzy and flat.
