But lately... especially on the nights before a run, it's a whole different story.\n\nI'll get into bed, usually around ten, ten-thirty, right after the late local news—I always like to catch the weather report, you know, just to see what kind of mess I might be driving into the next day—and I'll just lie there. I'll be trying to shut my brain off, but instead, I'm just running through the whole route in my head. I'll be thinking about the next day's stops, worrying if the loading dock at the warehouse in Des Moines is going to be backed up again, or if I need to take the bypass around Chicago because of that construction on 94... just all these little details that I shouldn't be sweating at eleven o'clock at night. \n\nAnd then, even when I do finally drift off, it's not a deep sleep. It's that light, choppy kind of sleep where you feel like you're half awake the whole time. And then, without fail, I'll wake up around four in the morning. Just... ping. Eyes wide open. The house is dead quiet, my wife is snoring softly next to me, and I'm just lying there in the dark. I'll try to go back to sleep, I'll flip the pillow over to the cool side, try to count backwards from a hundred, all those tricks, but it's no use. I just can't really get back to sleep. I just sort of doze and toss and turn until the alarm finally goes off at five-thirty. \n\nSo, by the time I actually get out of bed and stumble into the kitchen to brew that Folgers I was telling you about, I'm already exhausted. I mean, I still make it to work on time, I'm never late, I take pride in that. But I feel like I'm starting the day already worn down, you know? Like I'm running on a battery that only got charged up to maybe forty percent. It just makes that flat feeling I was talking about even heavier when you're dragging yourself through the day on four hours of bad sleep.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel tired or lacking in energy?\n\nPatient: Tired? Well... I mean, like I was just saying with the sleep thing, I definitely feel worn down from that. But as far as just generally lacking energy? I don't know. I'm not really sure I'd call it that. \n\nI mean, I'm fifty years old, and I drive a truck for a living. You sit in that cab for ten, eleven hours, staring at the white lines on the interstate, feeling the rumble of that big diesel engine right up through the floorboards... it kind of vibrates right into your bones after a few hundred miles. It takes it out of you. And sometimes, depending on the contract, I have to help unload. Like just last week, I was hauling a load of heavy-duty tractor parts down to Peoria, and the forklift operator at the receiving dock was on his lunch break. So I had to get back there in the trailer and start moving pallets around myself with a manual hand jack. By the time I was done, my shoulders were absolutely burning. \n\nSo, sure, I'm tired at the end of a shift, but I think anybody would be, you know? It's not like I'm falling asleep at the wheel or anything like that. I keep a big Stanley thermos of coffee with me—just black, no sugar, because sugar gives you that terrible crash later on, which I learned the hard way back in my twenties when I used to drink those giant fountain sodas from the gas station to stay awake. The coffee keeps me going just fine. I still get the job done, I still make my delivery windows. So I don't think I'm completely out of gas or anything. It's probably just... regular tired. Just the wear and tear of the road and getting older, I guess. Nothing out of the ordinary, really.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself moving or speaking more slowly than you used to?\n\nPatient: Moving or speaking more slowly? No... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, my wife always jokes that I talk too much as it is, so if I started slowing down, she'd probably throw a parade just to celebrate the peace and quiet. But seriously, no. You can't really afford to move slow in my line of work, anyway. \n\nWhen you're doing a pre-trip inspection on an eighteen-wheeler—which you have to do every single morning, it's strict DOT regulations, you absolutely cannot skip it—you're checking the air brakes, you're thumping the tires to check the pressure, you're looking at the fifth wheel coupling... you're climbing up and down, checking the kingpin, making sure the airlines aren't rubbing. If I was moving like molasses, I'd never get out of the yard on time. And time is money in freight, plain and simple. Dispatch is always breathing down your neck. My dispatcher, this guy Stan, he's a decent enough guy, but he's got a tight schedule to keep, you know? If I was dragging my feet and taking twice as long to get the rig rolling, he'd be blowing up my phone before I even hit the on-ramp for I-80. \n\nAnd as for talking... no, I talk just the same as I always have. I still get on the CB radio sometimes, though to be honest it's mostly just quiet these days, not like the old days when everyone was jawing on channel 19. But when I do talk to the guys at the truck stops, or to the receivers at the loading docks, I'm talking at my normal speed. I've been shifting those gears and watching those mirrors for so many years, my hands and feet just know what to do without me having to think too hard about it. And you see guys out there at the truck stops, sitting at the diner counters, staring at their coffee cups, just eating themselves alive with guilt because they missed their kid's high school graduation, or they weren't there for their wife's birthday because they were stuck in a white-out blizzard on Donner Pass. \n\nBut me? I never really let that stuff get to me in that way. I mean, my wife and I, we had an understanding from day one. She knew what she was signing up for when she married a trucker. I remember this one time, it was our tenth anniversary, and I was supposed to be home by Friday night. I had this whole plan to take her to this nice steakhouse down by the river. By the time I got rolling again, there was no way I was making it back. I ended up eating a microwaved burrito at a Love's Travel Stop at midnight. \n\nNow, some guys would beat themselves up over that for years. They'd feel so guilty they couldn't sleep. I've always worked hard, I've always provided, and I've always kept my nose clean. I don't have any dark secrets or terrible mistakes hanging over my head. I try to treat people right, do my job, and get the freight where it needs to go. So, no... I don't really have that guilt weighing me down. Two weeks? Well, Doc, if it was just a bad two weeks, I probably wouldn't be sitting here taking up your time today. Honestly, it's been a whole lot longer than two weeks. 

I actually finally made the appointment to come in because for a really long time now—pretty much ever since my dad passed—there's just been this... this heavy, low feeling sitting on me most days. Nearly every day, just like you asked. I mean, I still get things done, don't get me wrong. I'm not laying in bed pulling the covers over my head. I get up, I get through my driving routes, whether I'm hauling freight down I-81 or just doing local runs, and I still show up for my volunteer shifts down at the veterans' hall on Thursday nights. I don't call out, and I don't leave people hanging. My dad always taught me that you show up and do the work, no matter what's going on in your head. You honor your commitments. So I do. 

But even when I'm doing all that... even when I'm keeping busy and getting the job done, that heavy feeling is just right there, sitting square on my shoulders. It’s hard to put into exact words, but it’s like I’m just going through the motions instead of really being in my own life anymore. It's like I'm a passenger in my own cab, just watching the highway lines blur by, but I'm not the one actually driving the truck. I'm just physically present. And it doesn't ever really lift. It's not just a bad weekend here or there where you feel a little blue and then you snap out of it by Monday morning. It's just this constant, low weight that I'm carrying around, day in and day out, for months and months now.

The mortgage, the truck payments, all those manila folders I was telling you about... she hates doing the paperwork. She'd be completely lost trying to sort out the utility bills and the insurance premiums, and I take my responsibilities seriously. I always have. \n\nSo, no. I wake up, I brew the coffee—just regular Folgers, I don't mess with that expensive stuff—and I go to work. I'm not looking to end the trip early, I'm just... I'm just not enjoying the scenery as much as I used to, I guess. But checking out? No. Never crossed my mind.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this heavy, flat feeling?\n\nPatient: How long... well, if I really sit down and trace it back, I guess it's been about three years now. Yeah, three years. It started right around the time my dad passed away. \n\nThat was back in, let's see, it would have been early spring. March. I remember it was March because it was still freezing rain up in the panhandle where I was running a load of lumber, and the roads were just a miserable sheet of ice. I got the call from my sister while I was pulled over at a rest stop. He had been sick for a bit, it was his heart, so it wasn't a total shock, you know? But still, when it actually happens, it changes things. \n\nI took a couple weeks off work, which I almost never do—I hate leaving my dispatcher hanging—but I had to go help my mom sort out the house and the estate and all that. We had to sell his old Chevy pickup, which honestly broke my heart a little, but she couldn't drive a manual transmission and it was just going to sit there and rust in the driveway. Anyway, we got through the funeral, got the paperwork sorted, and after all the dust settled, I got back in my rig and went back to my routes. \n\nAt first, I figured I was just grieving, you know? Just feeling weighed down because of the funeral and losing the old man. Anyone would feel that way. But then spring turned into summer, and summer into fall, and we had the holidays without him, and that feeling... it just never lifted. It never went away. I kept thinking one morning I'd wake up, brew my coffee, and feel like my old self again—the guy who used to actually whistle while he checked his tire pressure in the morning. But it's been three whole years now of just... coasting. Just that same flat, heavy line every single day since we buried him. So, yeah, I'd say three years is about right.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past three years?\n\nPatient: Weight? No, not really. I mean, you'd think I would have, given the job. You sit behind the wheel of a rig for eleven hours a day, your metabolism isn't exactly doing jumping jacks, you know? And the food out there on the interstate... man, it's a disaster waiting to happen. You pull into a Love's or a Pilot, and it's all roller hot dogs that have been sitting there since the Bush administration, or those fast-food joints where everything is deep-fried. I see guys out there, other drivers, who have just ballooned up. They can barely climb up into the cab without losing their breath, and their knees are shot by the time they're forty-five. \n\nBut my wife, bless her, she tries to keep me in line. Pork chops, meatloaf, whatever. I don't really have the drive to go snacking late at night or anything, and I don't skip meals either. I step on it sometimes in the bathroom—it's one of those old analog ones, not the digital kind where the battery always dies when you actually want to use it—and it usually hovers right around 195. So, no, the weight hasn't really fluctuated at all. Just steady. Like everything else, I guess. Just staying exactly the same.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having any problems with your sleep?\n\nPatient: Sleep? Yeah, sleep's... well, it's not great. The house is dead quiet, my wife is snoring softly next to me, and I'm just lying there in the dark. It takes it out of you. And sometimes, depending on the contract, I have to help unload. My dispatcher, this guy Stan, he's a decent enough guy, but he's got a tight schedule to keep, you know? Just the usual.\n\nDoctor: Do you have trouble concentrating on tasks, like when you're driving or helping at the community center?\n\nPatient: Concentrating? Well, it's funny you ask that. You think about the past, you think about the folks who aren't around anymore. I shed more than a few tears gripping that steering wheel those first few months, I'll be the first to admit that. \n\nBut wanting to end it? Thinking about steering the rig into a bridge abutment or something crazy like that? Never. I've got my wife to get home to, I've got a house to maintain, and I've got a job to do. When you lose somebody, you just... you just keep the wheels turning, you know? You put it in gear and you keep moving forward because that's all you really can do. So, no, I haven't had any thoughts like that at all. Not even close.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this way, and has it been constant or have you had periods where you felt better?\n\nPatient: Well, let's see... if I look back at the logbook of my life, so to speak, I'd say it's been right about three years now. Yeah, three years this past fall. It all really settled in right after my father died. Like I was telling you before, about being down in Georgia with that load of frozen chicken when I got the call... ever since that day, it's just been this steady, unchanging feeling. \n\nYou asked if there are periods where I feel better, and, well... I wouldn't say I have these big highs and lows. It's not like driving a mountain pass out in Colorado where you're grinding your way up to the summit in low gear and then flying down the other side. It's more like... well, like I said earlier about the Texas panhandle. Just flat. For three whole years. \n\nI kept thinking, you know, maybe after the first anniversary of his death, things would pick up. People tell you that all the time. They say, \"Oh, the first holidays are the hardest, the first Thanksgiving, the first Christmas without him.\" And my wife, bless her heart, she really tried to make that first Christmas special. She made his favorite pecan pie, we got a bigger tree for the living room... but I just sat there in my armchair, looking at the lights, and I just felt... exactly the same. Flat. \n\nAnd then the second year rolled around, and the third, and I was out on the road, hauling freight up through the Midwest or down the Eastern seaboard, and I realized, huh, this feeling hasn't really lifted. It hasn't gotten worse, mind you. I'm still doing my job, still doing my pre-trip inspections, still paying the mortgage on time, but it hasn't gotten any better either. It's just been this constant, steady, low hum... kind of like the sound of a diesel engine idling when you're trying to sleep in the sleeper berth at a rest stop. You get used to it, you can function with it, but you're always aware that it's there, just humming away in the background. So, yeah, three years of just... this. Just a long, flat stretch of road since he passed.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself moving or speaking more slowly than you used to, or do you feel like you're speeding up and can't slow down?\n\nPatient: Moving slower? Or speeding up? No... no, I wouldn't say either of those. I mean, look, I'm fifty years old now, so I'm not exactly springing up into the cab like a jackrabbit the way I did when I was twenty-five and fresh out of CDL school, but I'm certainly not moving through molasses either. You know, you just get into a rhythm with this job. A steady pace. Like when I do my pre-trip inspection every morning out in the yard. I've got my routine, right? I start at the driver's side door, check the hinges, walk around the front, pop the hood, check the serpentine belts, make sure the oil and coolant levels are good, thump the steer tires... it takes me the exact same fifteen, maybe twenty minutes it's always taken me for the last couple of decades. I don't drag my feet doing it, I just get it done. \n\nAnd as for talking... well, my wife would probably tell you I can still talk the ears off a brass monkey once I get going, especially if you get me on a topic like those new electronic logging devices or the parking situation at the rest stops on I-95. But I don't think I'm speaking any slower or faster than I ever have. Just my regular speed. \n\nAnd feeling like I'm speeding up or can't slow down? Lord, no. Definitely not that. I see these young guys at the Flying J or the Pilot stations, bouncing around, hopped up on those big cans of Monster energy drinks, rushing to grab their roller grill hot dogs and sprinting back to their rigs like they're qualifying for the Daytona 500. That's just a good way to burn yourself out or make a stupid mistake. That's not me. Never really has been, and it certainly isn't now. I just... I just put it in cruise control, physically speaking. I keep my own engine right at a steady RPM, you know? So no, I don't feel sluggish like I can't get out of my own way, and I don't feel all revved up and restless either. I'm just operating at the exact same speed I always have. Just keeping it between the ditches.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're unable to experience pleasure from activities you once enjoyed?\n\nPatient: Well, unable to experience pleasure... that's a tricky one to answer, Doc. Because it's not like I don't enjoy anything at all anymore. It's more like... well, let me explain it like this. You take my old Ford pickup, right? A '78 F-150, cherry red, absolute beauty. I used to spend hours out in the driveway on a Sunday afternoon, polishing that chrome bumper until you could see your reflection in it clear as day. I'd have the radio on, listening to the ballgame, maybe sipping on a cold iced tea my wife brought out for me. And I loved it. I really did. It felt good to see that truck shine, knowing I put the elbow grease into it. \n\nNow? Well, I still wash the truck. I still get the bucket out, mix up the soap, get the sponge, and go over the whole thing. I don't let it sit there and rust or get covered in pollen and road grime. But when I'm out there doing it... it's just a chore now. I don't get that same kick out of it. I'm just going through the motions, you know? Just scrubbing the hood because the hood needs scrubbing, not because I'm looking forward to seeing it gleam in the sun. \n\nAnd it's not just the truck, either. My wife and I, we used to love going to this little diner out on Route 9 on Friday nights. They make this meatloaf that's just out of this world, with real mashed potatoes, not the instant stuff. We'd sit in our favorite booth by the window, watch the cars go by, and just enjoy a good meal after a long week on the road. We still go, mostly because she likes it, and I'm not gonna sit home and stare at the wall while she eats alone. But the meatloaf... it just tastes like food now. It fills the tank, so to speak, but I don't savor it the way I used to. \n\nSo, it's not that I can't do the things I used to enjoy, or that I've completely stopped doing them. I haven't locked myself in a dark room or anything drastic like that. I still go to the diner, I still wash the truck, I still watch the football games on Sunday. But the spark... that little bit of joy that used to come with those things... it's just sort of fizzled out. It's like listening to the radio when you're driving through a valley and the signal gets all fuzzy. You can still hear the song, you know the words, but the music just doesn't sound as good as it did when you had a clear signal. That's kind of how everything feels right now. Just... fuzzy and flat.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant changes in your appetite or eating habits over the past three years?\n\nPatient: Well, let me think on that. Changes in my appetite... no, I wouldn't say so. You know, when you drive a truck for a living, your eating habits are pretty much dictated by the interstates and the delivery schedule anyway. You've got your Pilot stations, your Love's, your TA travel centers, and you just sort of fall into a routine. \n\nFor the past three years... well, honestly, probably for the past fifteen years, my daily intake hasn't changed a lick. I wake up, I get my thermos of black coffee going, and I usually heat up one of those Jimmy Dean breakfast sandwiches in the microwave in the sleeper. The sausage, egg, and cheese ones—not the bacon, the bacon always gets too rubbery when you nuke it. Then for lunch, if I'm making good time and the weigh stations haven't held me up, I might pull over and grab a turkey sub or something, but usually, I just keep a bag of pretzels or some roasted almonds up in the cab with me and snack on those while I keep the hammer down. \n\nAnd like I was saying about that meatloaf at the diner with my wife... I still eat it. I still clean my plate every time we go. I'm not sitting there pushing my food around with my fork like a kid who doesn't want to eat his broccoli, and I haven't started binge-eating a bunch of junk food either. My stomach still rumbles right around noon just like clockwork, and I still eat my standard portions. I haven't lost any weight, haven't really gained a gut either—well, no more of a gut than a fifty-year-old guy sitting in a driver's seat for ten hours a day naturally gets, anyway. \n\nSo, no, no real changes in the appetite department. I still eat my three meals, still snack on my pretzels. Like I said before, the food just sort of fills the tank these days. I'm putting the fuel in the engine so the truck can keep rolling down the highway, even if I'm not exactly savoring the flavor of it all anymore. But the actual amount I'm eating, the times of day I'm eating... nah, that's all stayed exactly the same as it was before my dad passed. Steady as she goes.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any periods of at least two weeks where you felt depressed most of the day, nearly every day, since your father passed away?\n\nPatient: Two weeks? Well, Doc, if it was just a bad two weeks, I probably wouldn't be sitting here taking up your time today. Honestly, it's been a whole lot longer than two weeks. \n\nI actually finally made the appointment to come in because for a really long time now—pretty much ever since my dad passed—there's just been this... this heavy, low feeling sitting on me most days. Nearly every day, just like you asked. I mean, I still get things done, don't get me wrong. I'm not laying in bed pulling the covers over my head. I get up, I get through my driving routes, whether I'm hauling freight down I-81 or just doing local runs, and I still show up for my volunteer shifts down at the veterans' hall on Thursday nights. I don't call out, and I don't leave people hanging. My dad always taught me that you show up and do the work, no matter what's going on in your head. You honor your commitments. So I do. \n\nBut even when I'm doing all that... even when I'm keeping busy and getting the job done, that heavy feeling is just right there, sitting square on my shoulders. It’s hard to put into exact words, but it’s like I’m just going through the motions instead of really being in my own life anymore. It's like I'm a passenger in my own cab, just watching the highway lines blur by, but I'm not the one actually driving the truck. I'm just physically present. And it doesn't ever really lift. It's not just a bad weekend here or there where you feel a little blue and then you snap out of it by Monday morning. It's just this constant, low weight that I'm carrying around, day in and day out, for months and months now."
